why: Section 7.5.3(b) of this chapter states both halves of the rule: the ionization enthalpy decreases down a group, so the tendency to lose valence electrons and hence the metallic character INCREASES down a group; and the ionization enthalpy increases across a period, so metallic character DECREASES across a period. Locate the four elements: \(\mathrm{K}\) is in period 4, group 1; \(\mathrm{Mg}\) is in period 3, group 2; \(\mathrm{Al}\) is in period 3, group 13; \(\mathrm{B}\) is in period 2, group 13, directly above \(\mathrm{Al}\). \(\mathrm{K}\) is the furthest left and the furthest down, so it is the most metallic. Within period 3, \(\mathrm{Mg}\) lies left of \(\mathrm{Al}\), so \(\mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al}\). \(\mathrm{B}\) sits above \(\mathrm{Al}\) in the same group, so it is the least metallic of the four. The order is therefore \(\mathrm{K} > \mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al} > \mathrm{B}\). The other three options all fail: the first reverses the trend completely by putting \(\mathrm{B}\) first; the second places \(\mathrm{K}\), an alkali metal, last; the third places \(\mathrm{K}\) below \(\mathrm{Al}\), which contradicts the increase down a group. Option D states exactly this order.

Section 7.3.1 states it directly: on inspecting the electronic configurations of elements in the various periods, the period number is the same as the principal quantum number \(n\) of the outermost or valence shell. For example the second period begins with \(\mathrm{Li} : 1s^2 2s^1\) and ends with \(\mathrm{Ne} : 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\), every member having \(n = 2\) as its valence shell. The atomic number changes by one from element to element WITHIN a period, so it cannot be what the period number indicates; the atomic mass likewise varies along a period and is not what the modern table is built on (the modern periodic law is a function of atomic number); and the azimuthal quantum number \(l\) labels the subshell (s, p, d, f), which is what fixes the BLOCK, not the period. Option C, the principal quantum number, is therefore the correct choice.

Section 7.2 says that below the main table are placed two series containing fourteen elements each, and section 7.3.3 closes the f-block description with the statement that the f-block is placed separately at the bottom of the periodic table. The lanthanoids are one of those two f-block series (\({}_{58}\mathrm{Ce}\) to \({}_{71}\mathrm{Lu}\), section 7.4.4). The other three positions named in the options are already occupied: the left extreme of the table is the s-block (groups 1 and 2), the right hand side is the p-block (groups 13 to 18), and the middle is the d-block (groups 3 to 12). None of those can hold a fourteen-element series, because the main table has only eighteen groups. Option D, the bottom of the table, is where the lanthanides sit.

Table 7.1 of this chapter lists the general outer configuration group by group. \(ns^2 np^5\) is the entry for group 17, whose examples are \({}_{9}\mathrm{F} : 2s^2 2p^5\) and \({}_{17}\mathrm{Cl} : 3s^2 3p^5\), and section 7.4.2 names group 17 the halogen family. Testing the rejected options against the same table: alkali metals are group 1 with \(ns^1\); alkaline earth metals are group 2 with \(ns^2\); and the actinides are an f-block series at the bottom of the table, whose last electron enters an \((n-2)f\) subshell, so their outer configuration is not a p-subshell one at all. Only the halogens have seven valence electrons arranged as \(ns^2 np^5\), so option B is the correct choice.

Section 7.4.2 states that elements of group 17 form the halogen family, and Table 7.1 gives group 17 the outer configuration \(ns^2 np^5\) with \(\mathrm{F}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\) as its examples. The three rejected numbers can be ruled out from the same table: group 6 lies inside the d-block (groups 3 to 12), which section 7.4.3 says contains only metals, whereas halogens are reactive nonmetals; group 4 is likewise a d-block group; and group 2 is the alkaline earth metals with \(ns^2\), one of the two s-block groups on the extreme left. Option A, group 17, is therefore the correct choice.

Section 7.3.3 defines the s-block as the elements whose last electron enters an s-subshell, giving the general outer configuration \(ns^{1-2}\), so the s-block is exactly groups 1 and 2. Writing the configurations of each pair settles it. \({}_{3}\mathrm{Li} : 1s^2 2s^1\) and \({}_{12}\mathrm{Mg} : 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2\) both end in an s-subshell, so both are s-block. Of the rejected pairs, \({}_{7}\mathrm{N} : 2s^2 2p^3\) and \({}_{15}\mathrm{P} : 3s^2 3p^3\) are group 15, \({}_{6}\mathrm{C} : 2s^2 2p^2\) and \({}_{14}\mathrm{Si} : 3s^2 3p^2\) are group 14, and \({}_{9}\mathrm{F} : 2s^2 2p^5\) and \({}_{17}\mathrm{Cl} : 3s^2 3p^5\) are group 17 — every one of those six elements ends in a p-subshell and so belongs to the p-block. Option B, the pair 3 and 12, is therefore the correct choice.

Section 7.5.2(b) defines isoelectronic species as atoms and ions that contain the SAME NUMBER OF ELECTRONS, so each pair is settled by counting. \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) has \(11 - 1 = 10\) electrons while \(\mathrm{Na}\) has 11, so that pair is NOT isoelectronic. \(\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}\) has \(12 - 2 = 10\) and \(\mathrm{Ne}\) has 10, so that pair IS isoelectronic. \(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}}\) has \(13 - 3 = 10\) while \(\mathrm{B^{3\oplus}}\) has \(5 - 3 = 2\), so that pair is NOT isoelectronic. \(\mathrm{P^{3\ominus}}\) has \(15 + 3 = 18\) while \(\mathrm{N^{3\ominus}}\) has \(7 + 3 = 10\), so that pair is NOT isoelectronic either. The question as printed therefore has THREE options that correctly answer it, and only one isoelectronic pair among the four, so no single option can be marked as the answer. The chemistry to take away is the counting rule itself: add one electron for each unit of negative charge and subtract one for each unit of positive charge, then compare the totals.
solution: [Textbook misprint: this multiple-choice question is defective as printed — THREE of its four options correctly answer it, so no single option can be marked as the answer. Counting electrons, Na+ (10) and Na (11) are not isoelectronic, Al3+ (10) and B3+ (2) are not isoelectronic, and P3- (18) and N3- (10) are not isoelectronic; only Mg2+ (10) and Ne (10) are. The options are transcribed exactly as printed and no correct option has been marked.]

why: Section 7.3.2 explains that a new shell is added down a group, so the general OUTER electronic configuration repeats down a group, and section 7.5 adds that elemental properties show similarity within a group. Similar properties therefore mean same group. Writing the configurations: \({}_{13}\mathrm{Al} : 3s^2 3p^1\) and \({}_{31}\mathrm{Ga} : 4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^1\) — both end \(ns^2 np^1\), so both are group 13 and are expected to behave alike. The rejected pairs straddle different groups: \({}_{11}\mathrm{Na}\) is group 1 while \({}_{20}\mathrm{Ca}\) is group 2; \({}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}\) is group 2 while \({}_{10}\mathrm{Ne}\) is an inert gas of group 18; and \({}_{21}\mathrm{Sc}\) is a d-block element of group 3 while \({}_{33}\mathrm{As}\) is a p-block element of group 15. Option A, the pair 13 and 31, is therefore the correct choice.
